papers.title: [Editorial] Skin diseases: beyond the visible
papers.summary: Even the very word vitiligo denotes stigma—it probably comes from the Latin vitium, meaning a blemish, a defect, or a flaw. The visibility of depigmented skin, a culture that judges people by how they look, and enduring misconceptions of contagion have reinforced negative social attitudes towards the condition even while it is often dismissed as merely a cosmetic concern. This double injustice has left many who live with vitiligo socially and culturally shunned. But science has moved on, and a deeper understanding of vitiligo's pathophysiology—the immune-mediated loss of pigment-producing melanocytes—has enabled the development of new targeted therapeutics.

papers.title: [Comment] A novel unimolecular GLP1 and amylin receptor agonist for glucose and weight control
papers.summary: The therapeutic landscape of type 2 diabetes and obesity has evolved from single-hormone incretin modulation towards multireceptor metabolic engineering. Amylin is cosecreted with insulin from pancreatic β cells in response to food intake and acts on amylin receptors distributed across the brain, pancreas, adipose tissue, and gastrointestinal tract to regulate appetite, delay gastric emptying, and decrease glucagon secretion, providing multisite integrative control of energy balance.1,2 Notably, amylin receptors are heterodimeric complexes composed of a calcitonin receptor core and receptor activity-modifying proteins (RAMP1, RAMP2, or RAMP3).

papers.title: [Comment] Oral JAK inhibitors for vitiligo: a new era of innovation
papers.summary: Non-segmental vitiligo, a chronic immune-mediated depigmenting skin condition affecting millions of individuals worldwide, has long occupied a paradoxical position within dermatology.1 Despite its considerable impact on patients’ wellbeing and quality of life, it has historically been trivialised as merely a cosmetic condition.2 For many patients, particularly those with darker skin tones, vitiligo remains not only highly visible but deeply stigmatising, with consequences extending into social and professional life.

papers.title: [World Report] Afghan health under pressure 5 years after Taliban takeover
papers.summary: Restrictions on women and girls, deep cuts to international aid, health-facility closures, and mass returns are mounting pressure on Afghanistan's fragile health system. Sophie Cousins reports.

papers.summary: WHO's efforts to eliminate the disease are way off target. Sophie Cousins reports.

papers.title: [Perspectives] Pandemic emotions
papers.summary: There have been various efforts to capture public experiences and views during the COVID-19 pandemic, most frequently through surveys about perceptions of the risk of getting COVID-19, willingness to accept a COVID-19 vaccine, and attitudes towards government handling of the pandemic—from its policies around lockdown, school closures, and physical distancing to vaccine mandates and travel restrictions. But what was less captured in the multitude of pandemic surveys were records of the experiences and waves of emotions felt during the COVID-19 pandemic, written or recorded by citizens themselves.

papers.title: [Obituary] Naseem Salahuddin
papers.summary: Infectious disease specialist, rabies control advocate, and educator. Born on April 27, 1944, in Karachi, Pakistan, she died following a road traffic crash in Tangiers, Morocco, on May 22, 2026, aged 82 years.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Beyond the metaphor: what One Health must become
papers.summary: France's decision to anchor its 2026 G7 presidency around One Health signals a high point for this approach.1 Although the political energy is real, so is the risk of squandering it. Despite years of discussion, One Health is better at describing a vision than specifying what must change and for whom. The 2022 One Health High-Level Expert Panel definition speaks of balancing the health of people, animals, and ecosystems as parallel goods.2 The Berlin Principles affirm the intrinsic value of wildlife and ecosystem health independent of human utility.

papers.title: [Correspondence] AI for science: decoding complexity for planetary health
papers.summary: The planetary health system is extraordinarily complex, encompassing human communities, wildlife species, natural ecosystems, and diverse societal factors.1 Planetary health is constrained by boundaries and finite resources shared across generations.2 Without artificial intelligence (AI), fully tracking and simulating humanity's collective environmental footprint against planetary limits was an insurmountable challenge.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Time to apply Arctic dogs to polar One Health surveillance
papers.summary: The Arctic is undergoing rapid transformation driven by global warming, long-range transport of toxic industrial chemicals, emerging diseases, and biodiversity change, with cascading consequences for ecosystems and human health worldwide.1 Addressing these interconnected challenges requires integrated polar One Health surveillance.2 Arctic dogs are uniquely positioned for this role because they share ecological niches, environmental microbiomes, and marine-based dietary exposures with Indigenous communities across the circumpolar north.

papers.title: [Correspondence] The next global health architecture cannot exclude women
papers.summary: As we navigate the redesign of global health at a moment of acute constraint, one troubling reality stands out: the women who already effectively run our health systems are chronically underfunded as leaders. Women provide nearly 70% of health care globally but hold fewer than 25% of senior leadership roles.1 Women are under-represented in decision-making discussions where health policy and budgets are decided.2 This is not an equity problem; it is a matter of whether the next system has the shared leadership it needs to perform.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Semaglutide treatment fails but might prevent Alzheimer's disease
papers.summary: We read with interest Lon S Schneider's Comment1 on the evoke and evoke+ trials2 of oral semaglutide in early symptomatic Alzheimer's disease. While we agree that these studies do not support semaglutide as a treatment for established Alzheimer's disease, we caution against interpreting the findings as evidence against the broader preventive potential of GLP-1 receptor agonists.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Manufactured ruin: what the World Report on Cuba left unsaid
papers.summary: We read Joe Parkin Daniels’ World Report1 on Cuba's deepening health crisis with collegial concern about what remains structurally absent from its causal account. Missing is any serious reckoning with six decades of US embargo, expanded sanctions, a State Sponsor of Terrorism designation, and a complete fuel blockade.2 Taken together, these constitute one of the most sustained economic sieges in modern history, with a disproportionate impact on Cuban children.3,4 Such omissions are not neutral.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Ethics laundering and Cuba's health myth
papers.summary: Joe Parkin Daniels’ World Report1 rightly documents the worsening crisis in Cuban health care, but the crisis should not be read mainly through the regime's preferred explanation of external constraint. I am troubled that Cuba's health crisis is still described without naming with equal clarity the power that produced the country's structural vulnerability, administered it, and converted it into political alibi. The US embargo has served the regime mostly as a rhetorical shield: a real but partial external constraint inflated into a total explanation for a ruin whose core is internal.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Poor response from the Israeli Medical Association
papers.summary: I read with interest the World Report1 covering the campaign urging the World Medical Association (WMA) to suspend the Israeli Medical Association (IMA). The People's Health Movement was among the organisations that initiated this campaign.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Health care under fire: the need for medical leadership
papers.summary: The World Report, which discusses calls to boycott the Israeli Medical Association,1 and the insightful Perspective, written amid the ongoing destruction of southern Lebanon by Israel's Government,2 prompt fundamental questions about the role of medical leadership in times of war, crimes against humanity, and direct targeting of hospitals and medical personnel.3

papers.title: [Correspondence] Actions speak louder than words
papers.summary: As a member of the Israeli Medical Association, I am deeply disturbed by how medicine has become entwined with politics, as seen in the World Report.1 Criticism against Israel's Government should not be targeted against its doctors. The Israeli medical oath obligates extending a helping hand to the wounded and sick, whether friend or foe. However, actions speak louder than words. I am privileged to work every day, shoulder to shoulder, with Arab health-care workers and doctors, constituting a quarter of Israel's physicians.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Delegitimisation of national medical associations
papers.summary: We are disappointed that a campaign to selectively delegitimise and isolate Israeli physicians was publicised in a World Report,1 describing a petition to expel the Israeli Medical Association (IMA) from the World Medical Association (WMA). The untenable double standard advanced by the World Report is that an Israeli professional medical organisation should publicly adopt political and military positions for which it is clearly not responsible, to maintain its international standing. No comparable expectation is imposed upon other national medical associations.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Hate has no place in medicine
papers.summary: As National President of Hadassah, the Women's Zionist Organization of America, and Director General of its Israeli hospital system, the Hadassah Medical Organization, we are deeply troubled by the petition described in the World Report1—to expel the Israeli Medical Association (IMA) from the World Medical Association (WMA), of which the IMA is a founding member.

papers.title: [Articles] Efficacy and safety of once-daily oral zenagamtide, a novel unimolecular GLP-1 and amylin receptor agonist, in adults with type 2 diabetes: a multicentre, randomised, parallel, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-finding, phase 2 trial

The safety and tolerability of oral zenagamtide was consistent with other GLP-1 and amylin receptor agonists.

papers.title: [Articles] Efficacy and safety of once-weekly subcutaneous zenagamtide, a novel unimolecular GLP-1 and amylin receptor agonist, in type 2 diabetes: a multicentre, randomised, parallel, double-blind, placebo-controlled, dose-finding, phase 2 trial
papers.summary: In people with type 2 diabetes, once-weekly subcutaneous zenagamtide 0·4–40 mg demonstrated clinically meaningful and significant improvements in change in HbA1c from baseline to week 36 compared with placebo, with a safety and tolerability profile consistent with that of other GLP-1-based and amylin-based therapies.

papers.title: [Articles] Efficacy and safety of upadacitinib in adults and adolescents for treatment of non-segmental vitiligo (Viti-Up): results of two phase 3 randomised controlled studies

papers.title: [Editorial] Our twenty-five year journey
papers.summary: This August issue marks the 25th anniversary of The Lancet Infectious Diseases. The journal was created in 2001 by our late Editor-in-Chief John McConnell whose vision for a journal for specialists in infectious diseases that could inform public health decisions and clinical practice is alive to this day. John's curiosity and conviction that an infectious cause could always be found at the root of most medical problems shaped the growth of the journal from an initial collection of reviews to the multifaceted publication it is now.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Rapid recruitment for a remote long COVID clinical trial
papers.summary: There have been few long COVID clinical trials relative to the burden of disease,1 and even fewer have been accessible to people with more severe illness.2 As a person who has had moderate-to-severe long COVID (depending on the day) since 2020, I have long advocated for at-home access to clinical trials.3–5

papers.title: [Correspondence] Tuberculosis treatment with early detection
papers.summary: Recently, I was working in a densely populated informal settlement in Mumbai, a metropolitan city in India, where tuberculosis was a daily finding in my outpatient department due to the high endemicity. One case, however, stayed with me.

papers.title: [Correspondence] The limb-saving power of bedside Gram staining
papers.summary: As infectious disease physicians, we rarely have a single dramatic procedure that instantaneously changes a patient's trajectory: no emergent catheterisation for acute myocardial infarction, no urgent endoscopy for torrential upper gastrointestinal bleeding. Antibiotics can look deceptively simple—something any competent generalist can prescribe. Our value often appears only later, after the fever has lingered, the tests have failed, and someone finally asks, “What are we missing?” Even then, the resolution can feel quiet rather than cinematic.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Keep antibiotics habitable: stewardship as climate mitigation
papers.summary: Friends and family kept asking, “Why infectious diseases?” Although their intent was kind, the subtext was constant: why choose a path that is demanding, less lucrative, and often unseen? I had no slogan in response. I only knew that, since adolescence, I was drawn to infections caused by improbable microorganisms, with protean presentations and diagnostic challenges that leave no room for shortcuts. At first, microorganisms appear as unidentifiable, surreal shapes, until diagnostics and microbiology allow for their identification and characterisation.

papers.title: [Correspondence] 25 years of antibiotics: from desperate access to precision safety
papers.summary: As The Lancet Infectious Diseases approaches its 25-year anniversary, your Editorial1—and its call for stories of success, hope, and inspiration—resonated strongly with our team. In our intensive care unit (ICU), one such story began with an uncomfortable series of questions at the bedside: “Will tigecycline work?”, “Can we keep this patient safe while it works?”, and “Do we have any other options?”

papers.title: [Correspondence] The optimism in front of us
papers.summary: The world often feels dark when seen through today's headlines. Conflict, division, mistrust, and crisis compete for attention.1 However, working and training in infectious diseases offers a different daily perspective. Infection does not recognise age, gender, ethnicity, religion, borders, politics, or culture; it can affect any person and any organ system. Because of this, infectious diseases practice is, by necessity, collaborative and boundary-crossing.

papers.title: [Correspondence] The importance of study volunteers in saving future lives
papers.summary: We had just reviewed how the lymph node biopsy would be performed when I asked the study volunteer why he wanted to do it. Did he understand there would be no direct benefit, that the results were not going to improve his health? There were also risks involved, such as pain, bleeding, or infection.

papers.title: [Correspondence] Crossing the regulatory and clinical operational valley in antimicrobial resistance: from a start-up's perspective
papers.summary: The milestone that gave me the greatest satisfaction last year was not a headline-grabbing breakthrough, but the quiet alignment of two parallel worlds: regulatory clearance and operational readiness for BWC0977, a novel dual-targeting inhibitor of DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV—a class that has seen little innovation in decades.1 BWC0977, a broad-spectrum antibacterial clinical candidate, is currently undergoing a phase 1 trial in Australia.2 It demonstrates broad-spectrum activity against the major WHO-published list of bacterial priority pathogens.

papers.title: [Correspondence] A new era of hope: the impact of long-acting injectables for individuals ageing with childhood HIV
papers.summary: HIV carries an unwarranted stigma especially in perinatal and prepubescent populations.1 Thanks to the introduction of antiretroviral therapy (ART) during pregnancy, the rate of perinatal HIV transmission has decreased from 20–30% to 0·1–0·5%.2,3 In 2022, nearly 13 000 people in the US were living with perinatal HIV;4 these patients cannot be forgotten. For this perinatal population, daily medication is both beneficial and emotionally challenging. Daily medication can feel burdensome and overwhelming, leading to non-compliance or discontinuation; risking resistance, viraemia, mental anguish, and resentment.

papers.title: [Correspondence] A defining clinical moment during the COVID-19 pandemic in Nigeria
papers.summary: Moments that shape careers in infectious diseases are often rooted in uncertainty but clarified by experience. After passing my part one fellowship examination in internal medicine in May 2019, I remained undecided about whether to pursue a career in nephrology or in infectious diseases. This uncertainty was resolved by the emergence of COVID-19 in Nigeria in February 2020, and the rapid establishment of national response structures, including isolation and treatment centres across federal tertiary hospitals.

papers.title: [Newsdesk] Research in brief
papers.summary: Reverse-transcription quantitative PCR-based assays for orthoebolaviruses such as Ebola, Sudan, and Bundibugyo viruses are resource intensive and take several hours to provide results, highlighting the need for rapid point-of-care tests. Using previously generated murine monoclonal antibodies specific for orthoebolavirus glycoproteins, researchers in Canada developed a prototype immunochromatographic lateral flow assay to detect glycoproteins from all known orthoebolaviruses. In 10 μL of plasma or whole blood, the test detected Ebola, Sudan, and Bundibugyo virus recombinant glycoproteins at amounts of 62·5 ng or 31·2 ng.

papers.title: [Profile] Troy Grennan—getting anal cancer the attention it deserves

Later when doing his own studies in Toronto, Grennan would volunteer (and later work) at Casey House, a well-known hospice (and now large charity) for those dying from or seriously ill with HIV. He was shocked to find his former neighbour as one of Casey House's patients, and the neighbour sadly died from HIV complications. It was one of many experiences he had at Casey House that left him determined to make a difference for people living with HIV.

papers.title: [Clinical Picture] Ignatzschineria larvae and Staphylococcus aureus bacteraemia secondary to cutaneous myiasis of the face

papers.title: Ancient genomes reveal distinct human dispersals and social stratification in the settlement history of western Remote Oceania

Ancient DNA spanning the last 3,000 years from the Solomon Islands, Vanuatu, Fiji, and Tonga reveals the sources and timing of dispersals following the initial settlement and uncovers social practices of an early Fijian community that experienced recent Papuan-related gene flow.

papers.title: Brain perivascular macrophages regulate endothelial cell function via a cMAF-dependent transcriptional program in mouse and human
papers.summary: This study identifies cMAF as a key transcription factor that orchestrates the molecular crosstalk between brain perivascular macrophages and arteries, thereby sustaining cerebrovascular function in health and disease.

papers.summary: Polyamines buffer labile iron, restraining its reactivity to suppress ferroptosis. Their depletion raises labile iron and creates synthetic lethality with GPX4 loss, revealing polyamine metabolism as an endogenous regulator of iron homeostasis.

papers.title: Functional atlas of vertebrate viral RNA elements that stabilize RNA and enhance translation

By combining these superior alleles, buckwheat lines are developed with enhanced high-altitude adaptability and improved field yields.

papers.title: Trans-regulatory gene mapping prioritizes disease drivers in asthma
papers.summary: DANDELION is a causal mediation-inspired framework enabling the identification of disease-driving genes missed by existing approaches. Applied to asthma, DANDELION prioritizes two protein palmitoylation enzymes, revealing a therapeutically tractable pathway that is an important and previously unexplored mechanism underlying asthma pathogenesis.

papers.title: Hierarchical and context-dependent encoding of actions in human posterior parietal and motor cortex
papers.summary: Interpreting others' actions is widely thought to rely on mirroring, yet direct neurophysiological evidence in humans remains scarce. Using single-neuron recordings from motor and posterior parietal cortex in tetraplegic participants, this study reveals hierarchical, context-dependent action coding: motor cortex encodes intentions, while posterior parietal cortex links observed actions to goals.

papers.title: Convergent evolution of metabolic regulation governs redox adaptation in Toxoplasma
papers.summary: A protein called TgPRO enables the metabolic adaptation and survival of apicomplexan parasites such as Toxoplasma under oxidative and nutrient stress.

papers.title: The sex and reproductive plasticity of intestinal muscles instruct gut size
papers.summary: Adult intestinal size plasticity is driven not only by epithelial stem cells but also by remodeling of the surrounding visceral musculature. Sex- and reproduction-dependent muscle remodeling controls gut size and transit, revealing the intestinal muscle as an active regulator of adult organ adaptation.

papers.title: The structural basis for LRRK2’s activation and autoinhibition
papers.summary: Elevated kinase activity in leucine-rich repeat kinase 2 (LRRK2) is linked to Parkinson’s disease; this study shows that its ROC GTPase acts as a nucleotide-dependent molecular switch that regulates activation and autoinhibition and reveals how some but not all PD mutations disrupt this regulatory switch.

papers.title: Metabolic atlas of early human cortex reveals glycolytic remodeling and pentose phosphate pathway control of cell fate transitions

This study maps the metabolic landscape of the developing human cortex and identifies glycolysis and pentose phosphate pathway activity as key regulators of radial glia fate, controlling the generation of outer radial glia and inhibitory neurons.

papers.title: Distinct cellular phenotypes of language and executive decline in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
papers.summary: Beyond its motor dimension, ALS can also involve cognitive impairment, with affected domains varying across individuals. Rather than a single common disease process, this heterogeneity reflects regionally and cellularly distinct alterations in the prefrontal cortex that are only partially predicted by TDP-43 neuropathology.

papers.title: Ultrarapid deep 3D histology enables intraoperative mapping of glioma infiltration
papers.summary: ULTRA compresses 3D histology from days or hours to within 30 minutes by leveraging the chemical specificity of stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy through the synergistic development of rapid tissue clearing and unsupervised AI. The platform enables intraoperative visualization of glioma architecture and depth-dependent tumor infiltration margins.

papers.title: Milk osteopontin alters the infant microbiome to drive DC hematopoiesis and disease tolerance
papers.summary: Milk-derived osteopontin confers protection from viral or bacterial severe lower respiratory illness by altering the neonatal gut microbiome.

papers.title: Co-option of retrotransposons promotes antibody diversification
papers.summary: A longstanding mystery in antibody diversification is how AID specifically targets immunoglobulin V genes. Ancient LINE-1 retrotransposons embedded within the immunoglobulin locus provide a recruitment platform for the HUSH complex and AID to drive somatic hypermutation.

papers.title: Spatial atlas of the human brain vasculature reveals specialized cell ensembles
papers.summary: An integrative cell and spatial atlas defines the organizing logic of the adult human cerebrovasculature, providing a framework for studying how vascular cell states support brain function and shape neurological disease vulnerability.

papers.title: Dietary arginine drives codon-dependent MHC class I translation and improves immunity in colon tumorigenesis and respiratory viral infection
papers.summary: Arginine availability regulates arginyl tRNA levels and codon-dependent translation of MHC class I, tuning antigen presentation and shaping anti-viral and anti-tumor immunity.

papers.title: Basement membrane turnover controls cell shape
papers.summary: Basement membranes are scaffolds of proteins, like collagen, that give organs shape. During development, basement membranes must adapt to the growing organ. We infer how fast the basement membrane adapts by measuring collagen turnover. We find that perlecan, another basement membrane protein, regulates collagen turnover to control organ shape.

papers.title: CRISPR screens identify targets to rescue age-related T cell dysfunction in cancer
papers.summary: Dusp5 and Zfp219 serve as critical regulators of age-related T cell dysfunction, with the loss of either driving T cells into an effector-like state that improves tumor control through distinct mechanisms within the aged tumor microenvironment.

papers.title: Gasdermin E couples viral pyroptosis to lethal hepatic lipid accumulation
papers.summary: Wetland virus activates dual apoptotic cascades to trigger GSDME-dependent hepatocyte pyroptosis, which rewires cellular lipid metabolism and ultimately causes severe hepatic steatosis. Therapeutic targeting of this pyroptosis-metabolism axis alleviates lethal wetland virus infection in mice.

papers.title: Why machines don’t speak biology: Toward native biological language models
papers.summary: Advances in AI have shown promise in protein structural information, but in this perspective, the authors argue that biology’s true complexity—emergent, evolved, and irreducibly messy—demands more than bigger models or more data and that unlocking a genuine “biological” AI requires anchoring machine learning in canonical, process-based “world models,” rather than chasing a universal theory built from parts alone.

papers.title: Advancing cancer detection and treatment using longitudinal routine clinical data
papers.summary: Liu et al. develop Oncoformer, a multimodal transformer that reads routine laboratory tests and chest X-rays already collected in everyday care. Across more than 3.6 million individuals, it detects cancer, infers tumor stage, and stratifies treatment response and recurrence risk, pointing toward risk-adapted cancer care built on data already in hand.

papers.title: Dynamic dimer-of-dimers architecture defines Mg2+ transport in human CNNM4
papers.summary: Cryoelectron microscopy structures of human CNNM4 in distinct conformational states reveal how an unexpected dimer-of-asymmetric-dimers architecture mediates Mg2+/Na+ exchange and identify an intracellular acidic patch that may function in cellular magnesium sensing.

papers.title: An Oryza orphan gene confers trans-species drought tolerance
papers.summary: ROAD1 is an Oryza-specific orphan gene that co-opts conserved ABA signaling to enhance drought tolerance without obvious growth defects or yield penalty under normal conditions. Elite rice lines carrying its functional allele exhibited higher grain yield than controls under drought, and its heterologous expression enhanced drought tolerance across diverse angiosperms.

papers.title: Trichoderma swollenin activates AtABCB5-dependent auxin efflux to promote plant development
papers.summary: The beneficial fungus Trichoderma acts through the secreted swollenin ThSWO, which crosses the plant cell wall and engages AtABCB5, an auxin efflux carrier, at the host cell surface. This effector-transporter module tunes auxin-associated cellular responses, revealing how beneficial fungi co-opt host hormone transport to promote root development.

papers.title: Condensates of the chromatin regulator ANKRD11 restrict hypertranscribed genes to safeguard development
papers.summary: ANKRD11 restricts hypertranscribed genes by forming biomolecular condensates that spatially sequester elongation factors, with disruption of this condensate-mediated control leading to aberrant organogenesis and underlying the pathogenesis of developmental disorders like KBG syndrome.

papers.title: The intrinsic cardiac nervous system is essential for cardiac function and survival
papers.summary: Two genetically distinct neuronal subtypes in the intrinsic cardiac nervous system are differentially required for baseline cardiac function and stress resilience to maintain cardiac stability and survival.

papers.title: A domestication-selected enhancer coordinates source-sink balance to improve harvest index and yield in maize
papers.summary: A teosinte-derived enhancer boosts the harvest index and grain yield in maize by optimizing source-to-sink carbon and nitrogen allocation, revealing a physiological pathway to yield during maize domestication.

papers.title: Localized PD-1 CAR T therapy reprograms neuroinflammation
papers.summary: PD-1+ T follicular helper-like cells drive B cell-associated pathology in multiple sclerosis. Programmable PD-1-targeting CAR T cells selectively eliminate these pathogenic CD4 T cells while delivering IL-10 at sites of inflammation, thereby suppressing neuroinflammation across preclinical models.

papers.title: CSF clearance through arachnoid fenestrations to olfactory meningeal lymphatics
papers.summary: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) crosses arachnoid fenestrations near the olfactory bulbs to reach dural lymphatics that traverse the cribriform plate, connect to nasal lymphatics, and drain to cervical lymph nodes. Aging impairs this pathway, but intranasal VEGF-C restores the lymphatics and the CSF outflow.

papers.title: A bivalent molecular glue linking lysine acetyltransferases to oncogene-induced cell death
papers.summary: Chemically induced proximity of lysine acetyltransferases (KATs) with BCL6 reprograms epigenetic signaling to eliminate lymphoma tumors. Structural and mechanistic studies demonstrate that fortuitous protein-protein contacts convert proximity induction into targeted changes in chromatin, revealing a key mechanism by which small molecules can co-opt oncogenic transcriptional regulators to elicit malignant cell death.

papers.title: Viral protease-initiated lytic cell death as a universal antiviral mRNA therapy
papers.summary: VIDA mRNA enables universal broad-spectrum antiviral therapy by triggering viral protease-initiated lytic cell death to eliminate infected cells and activate protective immunity.

papers.title: Robust regulatory interplay of enhancers, facilitators, and promoters in a native chromatin context
papers.summary: Using an in situ genome-rewriting platform, Zhou et al. demonstrate that precise transcriptional regulation of the NMU promoter is governed by a 3D regulatory hub comprising a core retroviral LTR enhancer, a decoy LTR promoter, and activity-boosting “facilitator” elements.

papers.title: Skin-innervating glutamatergic neurons modulate aging
papers.summary: Within the skin, glutamatergic neurons expressing neurofilament heavy chain (Nefh) play a role in aging. Loss of Nefh during aging drives skin fibroblast senescence and collagen loss, whereas glutamate supplementation improves skin aging phenotypes.

papers.title: Strong, sustained type I IFN signaling acts cell intrinsically to impair IFNγ responses and cause tuberculosis susceptibility
papers.summary: Fattinger et al. reveal how an antiviral immune response impairs antibacterial immunity and causes tuberculosis susceptibility. Upon Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) infection, strong, sustained type I IFN signaling cell intrinsically suppresses IFNγ responsiveness, thus rendering macrophages permissive to bacterial growth. The results illustrate how Mtb exploits host immune pathways to promote pathogenesis.

papers.title: Cell-type-specific activation of broadly perceived effector-triggered immunity restricts pathogen invasion in plants
papers.summary: Chhillar et al. reveal that plant immunity is organized across leaf tissues through specialized cell-type programs. While a shared core immune program is broadly activated, individual cell types deploy distinct defenses. This spatial division of labor restricts pathogen invasion and explains immune coordination at single-cell resolution.

papers.title: Lactobacillus gasseri postbiotics ameliorate age-related decline in endometrial receptivity
papers.summary: Li et al. show that the age-associated loss of endometrial Lactobacillus is linked to impaired receptivity and identify Lactobacillus gasseri exopolysaccharides as candidate modulators of endometrial senescence and receptivity that act through Hippo-YAP signaling.

papers.title: Engineering oral commensal nanovaccines to activate mucosal-systemic immune cascades against tumor
papers.summary: Dong et al. develop a bacteria-based oral biohybrid vaccine that induces mucosal immunity and drives a mucosa-periphery-tumor immune cascade. Combined with PD-1 blockade, this strategy enhances effector immune cell trafficking, remodels the distal tumor microenvironment, and improves tumor control in multiple murine melanoma models.

papers.summary: (Immunity 25, 237–247; August 2006)

papers.title: UV irradiation drives lineage-specific MITF-mediated transcription of PD-L1 to confer immune tolerance to UV-mutated melanocytes
papers.summary: UVR-damaged melanocytes evade immune attack despite harboring many mutations. Lo et al. show that MITF, a transcriptional regulator crucial to melanocyte identity, directly induces the immune checkpoint molecule PD-L1. This intrinsic tolerance program shields melanocytes from T cells, limiting autoimmune melanocyte destruction and potentially enabling early melanoma immune escape.

papers.title: Coordinated transcriptional networks program organelle expansion and metabolic flows for high endothelial morphology and function
papers.summary: High endothelial venules require specialized morphology and PNAd expression to support lymphocyte homing; however, the transcriptional mechanisms coordinating these defining features have remained unclear. Bi et al. identify XBP1-dependent and CREB3L2-associated adaptive ER programs that couple organelle expansion with PNAd biosynthesis to drive HEV specialization and reveal conserved secretory programs shared with intestinal goblet cells.

papers.title: The genesis of cutaneous neurogenic inflammation is a multi-step process requiring dendritic cell aggregation
papers.summary: Neurogenic inflammation is an important component of cutaneous immunity, yet the mechanism remains incompletely defined. Chen et al. found that the neuropeptide substance P activates mast cell release of the chemokine CCL2 to form dermal aggregates of dendritic cells that are then efficiently activated by a second neuropeptide, CGRP⍺. Thus, initiation of neurogenic inflammation is a dynamic, multi-step process.

papers.title: Group 2 innate lymphoid cells activate myelin-reactive T cells to augment neuroinflammation
papers.summary: The meninges play a key role in central nervous system (CNS) inflammation and autoimmunity, but the mechanisms remain unclear. Huang et al. find that group 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s) accumulate in the dura during neuroinflammation, where they activate and expand myelin-reactive T cells, thereby augmenting neuroinflammation and CNS demyelination. Conditional deletion of H2-Ab1 in ILC2s diminishes neuroinflammation and CNS demyelination, highlighting ILC2s as a potential therapeutic target for restricting neuroinflammation.

papers.title: Virus-induced deconjugation of ISG15 dysregulates innate immunity and cellular metabolism
papers.summary: SARS-CoV-2 encodes a viral deISGylase called PLpro, but its physiological functions and direct substrates remain elusive. Using a deISGylation-activity-ablated recombinant SARS-CoV-2, Zhu et al. show that deISGylation activity is required for innate immune evasion and, furthermore, relieves metabolic restriction of viral replication by modulating the activity of key enzymes in glycolysis, the pentose phosphate pathway, and redox homeostasis.

papers.title: CD163+ red pulp macrophages interact with marginal metallophilic macrophages during blood-stage malaria to maintain splenic architecture
papers.summary: Splenic macrophages adapt to malaria through subset-specific remodeling and inter-macrophage communication. Using fate mapping, single-cell transcriptomics, and genetic perturbation, Mauel et al. show that red pulp macrophages (RPMs) and marginal metallophilic macrophages (MMMs) are predominantly yolk sac derived. They identify a CD163high iron-recycling RPM subset that is lost after malaria and find that stress response factor GDF15-dependent signaling supports MMM maintenance.

papers.title: Butyrophilin-like 3 and 8 tetramers clamp Vγ4Vδ1 T cell receptors for antigen-independent activation
papers.summary: BTNL3 and BTNL8 are butyrophilin-like receptors that selectively regulate intestinal Vγ4+ T cells, yet the underlying activation mechanism has remained elusive. Dong et al. reveal that BTNL3-BTNL8 forms an antigen-independent tetramer that drives γδ TCR dimerization and activation, providing a structural basis for tissue-specific immune surveillance.

papers.title: The transcription factor BACH1 couples chromatin priming and repression to enable macrophage plasticity and adaptation
papers.summary: Macrophage plasticity and function involve precise regulation of transcriptional programs. Tzerpos et al. find that the transcription factor BACH1 establishes early chromatin accessibility while maintaining transcriptionally repressive states in naive macrophages before activation. This dual activity—termed pioneer repression—regulates macrophage adaptation and inflammatory kinetics in vivo.

papers.title: Autophagy maintains high endothelial venule identity and function during inflammation
papers.summary: High endothelial venules (HEVs) facilitate lymphocyte entry into lymph nodes by displaying peripheral node addressin (PNAd), yet how PNAd is regulated remains poorly understood. Jacobs et al. reveal that autophagy preserves HEV identity and function by sustaining PNAd production. Loss of autophagy impairs lymphocyte recruitment, while targeting this pathway dampens inflammation in mouse models of psoriasis.

papers.title: Causal Language for Studies Using Difference-in-Differences Analyses
papers.summary: Many clinical investigations are intended to evaluate or demonstrate causal relationships (eg, the effect of a treatment or other intervention on patient outcomes), whether using information from well-designed randomized clinical trials, leveraging observational data with suitable methods, or combining the 2 approaches. Evaluating and communicating the degree to which a given study supports a causal conclusion can be complex, typically involving both clinical and methodological considerations, and using appropriate language to describe the relevant considerations—causal language—is critical. In 2024, a Special Communication in JAMA described a framework for causal inference and considered the implications of the framework for the use of causal language in medical journals, including JAMA and the JAMA Network journals.

papers.title: New Lungs for Lung Cancer—Perils and Promises
papers.summary: Despite the recent advances in systemic therapy, survival for patients with metastatic non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) without actionable genomic alterations in the tumor is limited. A small subset of patients with NSCLC have lung-only metastatic disease and often die of progressive lung failure. In this issue of JAMA, a study by Bharat and colleagues challenges an entrenched assumption that lung transplant has no role in the management of patients with advanced NSCLC with lung-only metastatic disease.

This result may be partly explained by the high proportion of patients with buprenorphine present in their urine prior to receiving either study intervention.

Here, we identify emperipolesis - the evolutionarily conserved process by which neutrophils pass through megakaryocytes - as a phenotypically transformative route of egress from bone marrow. By intravital microscopy and 3-D histology, we show that the rapid form emperipolesis is markedly enhanced under inflammatory conditions. Neutrophils exit from megakaryocytes directly to the blood, acquiring exosomes enriched in proteins related to metabolism, migration, and immune function. This transfer induces a distinct neutrophil phenotype characterized by enhanced glycolysis, oxidative phosphorylation, cytokine release, and longevity. Correspondingly, emperipolesis-educated neutrophils display accelerated migration in vitro and in vivo. papers.title: Single-cell analysis suggests coordinated immune-cell redistribution between blood and cerebrospinal fluid in early multiple sclerosis
papers.summary: Despite immune-cell infiltration being a hallmark of multiple sclerosis (MS), the interplay between the periphery and central nervous system immune responses is still incompletely characterized. We performed single-cell transcriptomic and V(D)J sequencing of paired blood and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) immune cells from treatment-naive relapsing-remitting women with MS and compared them to age- and sex-matched healthy controls. Across major immune lineages, we identified coordinated, compartment-specific immune alterations, with enrichment of activated and memory lymphocyte populations in the CSF and concomitant depletion of related populations in peripheral blood, suggesting their recruitment from blood to CSF. papers.title: Altered follicular immunity in secondary lymphoid organs is associated with interferon hyperactivity in Down syndrome
papers.summary: Down syndrome, caused by trisomy 21, is characterized by chronic interferon-associated inflammation and immune dysregulation, yet the contribution of human secondary lymphoid organs to shaping this immune landscape remains unclear. Using multimodal single-cell and spatial profiling of human tonsils, we identify extensive remodeling of immune organization in trisomy 21. CD4 T cells are skewed away from canonical follicular helper (TFH) programs toward inflammatory TFH1-like and cytotoxic helper states enriched for interferon-responsive transcriptional programs. Tonsillar TFH cells exhibit increased interferon-{gamma} and interleukin-21 production, indicating inflammatory skewing toward type 1 helper immunity. papers.summary: Inflammation is essential for regeneration yet can also drive fibroinflammatory remodeling; what determines these opposing outcomes remains unclear. papers.title: IL-17A Restrains Antiviral Immunity to Promote Chikungunya Virus Infection and Pathogenesis in the Heart
papers.summary: Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) infection is increasingly linked to cardiovascular complications, but the mechanisms underlying CHIKV-induced cardiovascular disease (CVD) remain unclear, and targeted therapies are lacking. Although elevated interleukin-17A (IL-17A) levels have been reported in CHIKV patients and associated with cardiovascular pathology, its role in CHIKV-induced cardiac disease is poorly defined. papers.title: Tuberculosis prevalence among children with severe acute malnutrition: a systematic review and meta-analysis
papers.summary: Introduction: Control of tuberculosis (TB) in children remains a major challenge globally. There is growing recognition that children with severe acute malnutrition (SAM) are a high-risk population for TB, but the global burden of TB in this group has never been comprehensively quantified. Methods: We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis to estimate the prevalence of TB among children with SAM. Following PRISMA guidelines, we searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, and WHO Global Index Medicus from database inception to June 15, 2026. We included studies reporting TB among systematically sampled cohorts of children <15 years with SAM as defined by the World Health Organization. papers.summary: Background Uganda is among the African countries most affected by the ongoing clade Ib Mpox (monkeypox) outbreak, with sustained community transmission since 2024. Effective community-level prevention depends on understanding how risk and protective factors are distributed across the social ecology. We applied a socio-ecological framework to map the determinants of Mpox transmission risk and protective practice in affected districts. Methods We conducted a multi-district, community-based cross-sectional survey of 3,960 community members aged 15-65 years across high- and low-burden districts in Uganda between February and March 2025. Participants were selected by multistage sampling and interviewed using a structured tool administered on tablets. papers.title: Burden and Seasonal Variations of Cutaneous Leishmaniasis in Afghanistan During 2024.
papers.summary: BackgroundCutaneous leishmaniasis (CL) remains a major neglected tropical disease in Afghanistan; however, recent nationwide evidence on its geographical and temporal distribution is limited. This study assessed the reported burden, spatial distribution and seasonal variation of cutaneous leishmaniasis across Afghanistan during 2024. MethodsA nationwide retrospective ecological study was conducted using aggregated routine surveillance data obtained from the National Malaria and Other Vector-Borne Diseases Program. All cases reported from government health facilities across Afghanistans 34 provinces between 1 January and 31 December 2024 were included. Reported incidence rates were calculated per 10,000 population using national and subnational population estimates. This study evaluated a sequencing strategy for WNV surveillance using these samples. papers.summary: BackgroundNontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM) are an increasingly common group of pathogens that remain challenging to diagnose and treat effectively. papers.title: Predicting undiscovered non-human primate hosts of Semliki Forest complex Alphaviruses
papers.summary: Arthropod-borne Alphaviruses in the Semliki Forest (SF) virus complex, including Chikungunya virus, Mayaro virus, and Onyong-nyong virus, represent a substantial threat to human health globally. These antigenically related viruses often cause short-term febrile symptoms that can progress to chronic and debilitating arthropathy. The ecology of these viruses is complex due to the involvement of various animal hosts and mosquito vectors in their transmission cycles. Non-human primates (NHPs) have been identified as potentially important animal hosts that may contribute to ongoing transmission and emergence, but the full range of known NHP hosts is not clear. papers.summary: BackgroundRetail red meat may act as a source of foodborne pathogens, antimicrobial-resistant bacteria, and antibiotic residues, posing a significant public health concern in Bangladesh. papers.summary: IntroductionResearch demonstrates neurodevelopmental differences in children who are HIV-exposed, but uninfected (CHEU) compared to their peers born unexposed. CHEUs are at higher risk for prematurity and low birth weight, both known risk factors for developmental delays. Despite increasing evidence, HIV exposure remains underrecognised as a risk factor for poor development by policy-makers and early childhood development (ECD) programs. We trialed an ECD intervention for CHEUs based on the Nurturing Care Framework developed by WHO, UNICEF, and the World Bank to improve neurodevelopmental outcomes in this vulnerable population. DesignWe conducted a randomized controlled trial of an ECD intervention for mothers living with HIV and their children born HIV-exposed, aged six to 24 months, living in peri-urban Lusaka. MethodsWe developed MALDI-ST, a convolutional neural network-based approach for strain typing. papers.title: Clinical outcomes of early aspirin versus non-aspirin NSAID use in adults hospitalized with influenza: A retrospective study
papers.summary: Seasonal influenza remains a major cause of morbidity and mortality worldwide. Although neuraminidase inhibitors improve clinical outcomes, influenza-related deaths persist. We evaluated the associations of early aspirin and non-aspirin nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) use with clinical outcomes in adults hospitalized with influenza. This retrospective study included adults admitted to the University of Minnesota Medical Center from 2016 to 2018. Among 2,816 patients screened, 320 had laboratory-confirmed influenza. papers.summary: BackgroundTuberculosis (TB) preventive treatment is a key component of TB control in low-incidence settings, but uptake remains low. ObjectiveTo explore factors influencing patient decisions to accept or decline preventive treatment for TB infection. This approach has been recently recommended by the World Health Organization for use with low-complexity nucleic acid amplification TB diagnostics to increase access to testing when resources are constrained. Pooled testing can also be used with novel near point of care tests, and evidence is needed on diagnostic performance of pooled testing in these more portable, lower cost tests. papers.summary: Autoantibodies neutralizing type I IFNs (AAN-IFN-I) have been found in significant proportions of cases of severe, critical, and fatal COVID-19 pneumonia. papers.summary: BackgroundVector-borne diseases (VBDs) are an evolving public health concern in Switzerland, where endemic tick-borne infections coexist with emerging mosquito-borne threats linked to climate and ecological change. Public preparedness depends on population knowledge, risk perception, and preventive behaviour alongside institutional capacity. We assessed knowledge, attitudes, and practices (KAP) regarding VBDs among adults in the canton of Bern, interpreted alongside a complementary national stakeholder survey. After validity screening, we derived a latent knowledge score using a two-parameter logistic item response theory (IRT) model fitted to knowledge items. papers.summary: BackgroundBlood culture-negative infective endocarditis (BCNIE) poses a significant diagnostic challenge. This study evaluated a multimodal diagnostic algorithm combining serological and molecular methods at the Argentine National Reference Laboratory. MethodsA prospective analysis was conducted on 53 consecutive patients with suspected BCNIE referred between January 2019 and December 2024. Dihydroartemisinin-Piperaquine (DP) is highly efficacious but there are concerns about widespread use given emerging artemisinin resistance and its role as an alternative first line treatment. papers.summary: BackgroundDrug-resistant tuberculosis (DR-TB) remains a major challenge to tuberculosis control in sub-Saharan Africa. Cameroon faces substantial challenges in managing DR-TB; however, national evidence on treatment outcomes remains unsynthesized. This systematic review and meta-analysis aimed to estimate pooled treatment outcomes, adverse drug events (ADEs), and predictors of unfavorable outcomes among patients with DR-TB in Cameroon. AMR development will depend in part how doxy-PEP changes rates of antibiotic use. papers.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to transform healthcare, with advanced multimodal approaches showing great promise in leveraging diverse health-related data. Here, we applied multimodal AI to entire electronic health record (EHR) and complete pathogen genome data to predict patient outcomes from life-threatening infection. An automated, scalable pipeline was developed for EHR data preprocessing, quality control, and standardisation.
